teile.einleitung: A windsock is a fabric tube that hangs from a mast. It shows at a glance where the wind is blowing from and how strong it is. You find it mainly at airfields and on bridges.
wichtigste: A windsock is compulsory at airfields.
Windsocks are usually striped red and white.
The tip points to where the wind is blowing.
When the windsock is fully stretched out, a strong wind is blowing.
At about 28 km/h it is completely filled at the airfield.
Aeroplanes take off and land into the wind.
On high bridges windsocks warn of crosswinds.

abschnitte.text: A **windsock** is a cone-shaped tube made of **fabric**. It hangs from a mast and can turn freely. The wind blows into the large opening and inflates the sock. That is why the tip points in the direction **towards which** the wind is blowing. So the opening points to where it comes from. Only because it is made of fabric can the wind inflate and turn it.

The stronger the wind blows, the more it fills the windsock. If it hangs limply, there is almost no wind. If it is **fully stretched out**, a strong wind is blowing. According to a rule of thumb in aviation, the windsock is completely filled at about **15 knots**. That is around **28 kilometres per hour**. The stripes help to estimate the wind strength roughly.

A windsock is compulsory at **airfields**. Pilots need to know the **wind direction**, because aeroplanes take off and land **into the wind** whenever possible. A headwind gives the aeroplane more lift on take-off and slows it down on landing. That is why the runway that best faces into the wind is used. Windsocks are usually striped **red and white** or orange and white, so that they can be seen clearly against grass and sky even from the air.

Sometimes there are windsocks on **motorway bridges** and high roads too. There strong **crosswinds** can endanger cars, lorries and motorbikes. The windsock shows drivers that they need to be careful. Often there is also a crosswind warning sign next to it.

gewusst: A knot is one nautical mile per hour, which is about 1.85 kilometres per hour.
At night windsocks are lit up at many airfields.

teile.einleitung: Volcanism covers all the processes in which molten rock from inside the Earth reaches the surface. These include volcanic eruptions, but also hot springs, geysers and gas vents. Volcanism has shaped the Earth, created ocean floors and islands and even changed the climate.
wichtigste: Volcanism occurs mainly at plate boundaries and above hotspots.
Shield volcanoes typically form from runny basaltic lava, as on Hawaii.
Stratovolcanoes such as Vesuvius are often explosive because their magma is rich in silica, thick and full of gas.
A pyroclastic flow is a hot avalanche of gas, ash and rock.
A volcanic mudflow of ash and water is called a lahar.
The island chain of Hawaii was formed by hotspot volcanism.
The eruption of Tambora in 1815 led to the “Year Without a Summer” in Europe and Switzerland in 1816.

abschnitte.text: Most volcanoes lie at **plate boundaries**. Where plates drift apart, as at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, runny magma rises. Where one plate sinks beneath another in **subduction**, rock melts at depth and feeds explosive volcanoes. Many such subduction zones lie on the **Pacific Ring of Fire** around the Pacific, for example in Japan, Indonesia, Alaska and the Andes. Most volcanism happens unnoticed under the sea.

Some volcanoes lie in the middle of a plate. There hot rock rises like a column from great depth; this is called a **hotspot**. The plate slowly moves over the hotspot, and so over time a whole chain of volcanic islands forms. The best-known example is Hawaii, where the oldest islands lie in the north-west and the youngest, active island in the south-east. Iceland and Yellowstone National Park in the USA also lie above hotspots.

Runny **basaltic lava** forms flat, wide shield volcanoes such as Mauna Loa on Hawaii. Their eruptions are usually calm. **Stratovolcanoes** such as Vesuvius or Fuji, on the other hand, are steep and built up from layers of lava and ash. Their magma is rich in silica, thick and full of gas, so they can explode violently. After very large eruptions the summit can collapse and form a caldera.

A **pyroclastic flow** is a hot avalanche of gas, ash and rock that races down a volcano’s slope at high speed. A volcanic mudflow of ash and water is called a **lahar**. Lahars form, for example, when an eruption melts glacier ice on the summit. In 1985 a lahar on the volcano Nevado del Ruiz in Colombia buried the town of Armero, and more than 20,000 people died. Poisonous gases and ash in the air are dangerous too.

In April 1815 **Tambora** on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa erupted, one of the strongest eruptions of the last few centuries. It hurled huge amounts of ash and sulphur into the atmosphere, which weakened the sunlight. In Europe the year 1816 was therefore cold and wet; it is called the **Year Without a Summer**. In Switzerland there were failed harvests and a famine, especially in eastern Switzerland. On Lake Geneva, during this gloomy summer, Mary Shelley wrote the story of Frankenstein.

Volcanism is not only dangerous. Volcanic soils are very fertile, which is why citrus fruits and grapes for wine grow on Etna. In Iceland **geothermal heat** is used for heating and for producing electricity. Hot springs and geysers such as Strokkur in Iceland attract many visitors. Over millions of years volcanism has also supplied gases for the atmosphere and water for the oceans.

begriffe.erklaerung: Place where hot rock rises from great depth and creates volcanoes in the middle of a plate.
Steep volcano made of layers of lava and ash that often erupts explosively.
Volcanic mudflow of ash and water.
Large basin that forms when a volcano collapses after an eruption.
Hot spring that shoots out a fountain of water at intervals.

gewusst: Measured from the seabed, Mauna Loa on Hawaii is higher than Mount Everest.
Around three quarters of all volcanic eruptions on Earth take place under water.
The word volcano comes from Vulcan, the Roman god of fire and of blacksmiths.

teile.einleitung: At a warm front, warm air pushes against colder air. Because warm air is lighter, it slowly glides up over it. Broad layers of cloud form, from which it often rains for a long time.
wichtigste: At a warm front, warm air glides over cold air.
The boundary between the air masses slopes very gently.
High feathery clouds often announce the front a day in advance.
Nimbostratus clouds bring long-lasting, steady rain.
Air pressure falls ahead of a warm front.
On weather maps it is a red line with semicircles.
A halo around the Sun can show that a warm front is approaching.

abschnitte.text: At a **warm front**, warm air meets cold air that is still lying near the ground. The warm air is lighter and slowly rises over the cold air. Experts call this **overrunning**. The boundary is **very gently sloping**: over 100 kilometres it often rises by only about one kilometre. That is why the clouds reach far ahead of the actual front.

abschnitte.titel: The clouds come one after another
abschnitte.text: First, fine **feathery clouds**, the cirrus, appear high in the sky. They often announce the warm front a day in advance. Then veil clouds make the sky milky. Their ice crystals bend the sunlight, and sometimes a bright ring forms around the Sun, a **halo**. Later the clouds become thicker and lower. Finally comes **nimbostratus**, a thick grey layer of cloud with no clear shape.

Nimbostratus brings **long-lasting, steady rain**, and in winter snow too. This kind of rain is called **steady rain** or, in German, Landregen. It is usually not as heavy as a thunderstorm downpour, but it often lasts for many hours. Ahead of the warm front the low is approaching, so the **air pressure falls** slowly and steadily. Once the front has passed, it usually becomes milder.

On weather maps a warm front is drawn as a **red line with semicircles**. The semicircles point in the direction in which the front is moving. Red stands for the warm air that follows. A cold front, on the other hand, is drawn in blue with triangles. Warm and cold fronts usually belong to the same **low** and move across the country with it.

gewusst: A halo is usually about 22 degrees away from the Sun.
A warm front is often followed by the warm sector and later by a cold front with showers.

teile.einleitung: In the past some people kept a tree frog in a jar and hoped it would reveal the weather. That is where the German word Wetterfrosch, “weather frog”, comes from. Today the word is also used jokingly for weather experts.
wichtigste: In the past, a tree frog kept in a jar was used as a weather frog.
There was a small ladder in the jar.
If the frog sat at the top, people expected fine weather.
The frog follows the insects and shows only the current weather.
In Switzerland all frogs are protected.
MeteoSwiss is the federal weather service.
The weather prophets of the Muota Valley forecast the weather from signs in nature.

abschnitte.text: In the past people put a **tree frog** in a large jar. Inside stood a small **ladder**. People looked to see whether the frog was sitting at the top or the bottom. If it climbed up, they expected **fine weather**. If it sat at the bottom, they reckoned on rain. This custom gave the **weather frog** its name.

A tree frog cannot predict the weather. When it is sunny, **insects** fly higher, and the frog climbs after them to catch them. So at most it shows the **current weather**. Besides, a jar is not a good place for a frog to live. In Switzerland all frogs are **protected**, and you must not simply catch a tree frog. It has also become rare.

The tree frog is small and usually **bright green**. It has **sticky pads** on its toes. With them it climbs skilfully on leaves, bushes and reeds. In summer it likes to sit in the sun. The male has a vocal sac on its throat and calls very loudly at night. It lives in areas with ponds and lots of bushes.

People who explain the weather on television or radio are sometimes jokingly called **weather frogs** in German. In Switzerland **MeteoSwiss** is the federal weather service. It measures the weather in many places, calculates forecasts and warns of severe weather. The **weather prophets of the Muota Valley** (Wetterschmöcker) in the canton of Schwyz work quite differently. They watch animals, plants and old signs in nature and make their forecasts twice a year.

gewusst: In calm weather the calls of a tree frog can be heard more than a kilometre away.
The Wetterschmöcker meet for their forecasts at gatherings that attract many spectators.

teile.einleitung: Water is the most important substance for all life on Earth. It covers most of our planet and occurs as a liquid, as ice and as steam. Switzerland is so rich in water that it is called the “water tower of Europe”.
wichtigste: Water is made of molecules with two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, chemically H2O.
Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
Most of the Earth’s surface is covered with water.
Only about 3 per cent of the water on Earth is fresh water.
No living thing can survive without water.
Switzerland is called the “water tower of Europe” because many large rivers rise here.
Ice floats on water because it is lighter than liquid water.

abschnitte.text: Water is a clear liquid with no smell and no taste. Its smallest particles, the **molecules**, consist of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom, so the chemical formula is **H2O**. Water can dissolve many substances such as salt or sugar. That is why it is never completely pure but usually contains minerals. Water is everywhere on Earth: in seas, lakes, rivers, in the ground, in the air and in all living things.

Water occurs in three **states of matter**. Below 0 degrees Celsius it freezes into solid ice; at 100 degrees Celsius it boils and turns into steam. These values apply at sea level; on a high mountain water boils at a lower temperature. A special feature is that water is heaviest at 4 degrees and ice is lighter than liquid water. That is why ice floats on top and lakes freeze from the top down, so that fish can survive at the bottom.

About 71 per cent of the Earth’s surface is covered with water, which is why the Earth is also called the **blue planet**. Around 97 per cent of it is salt water in the seas. Only about 3 per cent is **fresh water**, and most of that is frozen as ice in glaciers and at the poles. So only a tiny part of the water on Earth can be used directly by people.

Large rivers such as the **Rhine**, the Rhône, the Inn and the Ticino rise in the Swiss Alps. Their water flows into the North Sea, the Mediterranean and, via the Danube, the Black Sea. That is why Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**. Many lakes and glaciers store large amounts of fresh water. Around 6 per cent of Europe’s fresh water reserves are in Switzerland.

An adult’s body is about 60 per cent water, and in babies it is even more. Every day we lose water through sweating, breathing and going to the toilet. That is why children should drink about one to one and a half litres a day, preferably water. Plants are also mostly made of water; a cucumber, for example, is more than 90 per cent water.

In Switzerland clean **drinking water** comes straight out of the tap; it comes mainly from groundwater and springs. We need water for drinking, cooking, washing and flushing the toilet. Hydropower stations on rivers and reservoirs supply around 60 per cent of Switzerland’s electricity. Even so, it is worth saving water and keeping waters clean, for example by not pouring oil or medicines down the drain.

begriffe.erklaerung: Smallest particle of a substance, made of several atoms.
Form in which a substance occurs: solid, liquid or gas.
Water with very little salt, as in lakes, rivers and groundwater.
Nickname for Switzerland, because many of Europe’s large rivers rise here.

gewusst: If you poured all the water on Earth into a bathtub, the drinkable fresh water in it would be only a few spoonfuls.
A drop of water in the Rhine can travel more than 1200 kilometres from the Alps to the North Sea.
Under certain conditions hot water can freeze faster than cold water; this is called the Mpemba effect.

teile.einleitung: A volcanic bomb is a lump of lava that a volcano hurls through the air during an eruption. It cools down in flight and falls back to the ground as a chunk of rock. Volcanic bombs can be as small as a fist or as big as a car.
wichtigste: Volcanic bombs are lumps of lava that fly through the air.
In flight their outside cools down and becomes solid.
Many bombs are round or spindle-shaped.
Smaller stones are called lapilli.
In breadcrust bombs the surface cracks open.
Volcanic bombs are heavy and hot and therefore dangerous.

abschnitte.text: During an eruption, large **gas bubbles** burst in the lava. This makes a loud bang and hurls scraps of lava high into the air. They fall back down as **volcanic bombs**. In the air the outside cools down. So when it lands, the bomb is already fairly solid, but inside it can still be hot. Chunks larger than about 6 centimetres count as volcanic bombs.

The lump of lava spins as it flies. That is why it often becomes round or pointed at the ends like a **spindle**. Sometimes gas bubbles inside expand during flight. The already solid surface then cracks open. Such a bomb looks like a loaf of bread with a crust and is called a **breadcrust bomb**.

Not everything a volcano throws out is big. Smaller stones are called **lapilli**. The word is Italian and means “little stones”. They are about the size of peas to nuts. Even finer particles make up **volcanic ash**. All these pieces together are called ejecta.

Many volcanic bombs are **the size of a fist**, but some are huge, as big as a car. They can be heavy and very hot. Anyone who is hit can be seriously injured. That is why you must not go near the **crater** during an eruption. At active volcanoes there are exclusion zones that must be respected.

gewusst: Large volcanic bombs can fly several kilometres.
On Stromboli in Italy small scraps of lava are thrown out almost all the time.

teile.einleitung: A weather map shows at a glance what the weather is like over a large area at the moment. On it you can see highs, lows, fronts, wind and clouds. Experts use it to forecast the weather for the next few days.
wichtigste: A weather map shows measurements from many places at the same time; this is called synoptic.
Air pressure is converted to sea level.
Next to H or L stands the air pressure at the centre in hectopascals.
An occlusion is usually drawn in purple.
Wind barbs show wind direction and wind strength.
Cloud cover is given in eighths.
In the 19th century the telegraph made the first up-to-date weather maps possible.

abschnitte.text: A weather map is **synoptic**. The word comes from Greek and means “seeing together”. Measurements from many places at the **same time** are shown together. Only in this way does an overall picture of the weather situation emerge. This became possible in the 19th century thanks to the **telegraph**. With it, readings could be sent quickly to one place and drawn on a map the same day.

A station in the mountains always measures lower air pressure than one in the valley. That is why the pressure for the surface weather map is converted to **sea level**. Only then can the places be compared and the real **highs** and **lows** be recognised. On German maps they are marked H and T, on English ones H for “high” and **L** for “low”. Next to them stands the central pressure in **hectopascals**, for example 1035 for a strong high or 975 for a deep low.

Fronts are shown with lines and symbols. The **warm front** is red with semicircles, the **cold front** blue with triangles. The **occlusion** forms when the cold front catches up with the warm front. That is why it is drawn in the mixed colour **purple**, with triangles and semicircles at the same time. The symbols always point in the direction in which the front is moving.

The wind is shown with a **wind barb**. The arrow shows where the wind is blowing from, and small strokes at its end give the **wind strength**. Cloud cover is given in **eighths**, also called oktas. For this, meteorology divides the sky into eight parts. 0 eighths means cloudless, 8 eighths means completely overcast. On the map a small circle shows how much of it is filled in.

gewusst: Lines of equal air pressure on a weather map are called isobars.
When the isobars are close together, there is usually a strong wind.

teile.einleitung: Heat lightning is the name for the flashing of lightning from a faraway thunderstorm. You see the light but hear no thunder. Here it is often seen on warm summer evenings.
wichtigste: Heat lightning is lightning from a faraway thunderstorm.
You do not hear the thunder because the storm is too far away.
Thunder can usually only be heard up to about 15 to 20 kilometres away.
Often you only see the reflection of the lightning in the clouds.
Heat lightning is seen mainly at night, low on the horizon.
If you suddenly hear thunder, seek shelter at once.

abschnitte.text: With **heat lightning** you see the light of lightning that is very far away. It is perfectly normal **thunderstorm lightning**. Often the flash itself is hidden behind clouds or below the **horizon**. Then you only see the clouds briefly light up. This is called the **reflection**. Because the storm is so far away, it usually flashes low on the horizon.

Light is very fast and travels far. The sound of **thunder**, on the other hand, does not carry so far. You usually only hear it up to about **15 to 20 kilometres** away. The light of the lightning can be seen much further. That is why with heat lightning you only see the flashes and hear nothing. Mountains, wind and noises around you can also swallow up the thunder.

Here thunderstorms happen mainly in **summer**, when the air is warm and damp. In the evening and at **night** you can see their distant glow clearly in the dark sky. In bright daylight, on the other hand, the faint glow is hardly noticeable. Sometimes the sky flickers again and again for minutes while it stays completely calm where you are.

Heat lightning itself is harmless, because the storm is far away. But storms can come closer. If you suddenly hear **thunder**, the storm is close enough for lightning to strike. Then seek **shelter** at once in a building or a car. Outdoors, avoid lone trees, hilltops and water.

gewusst: If you count the seconds between the lightning and the thunder and divide by three, you get roughly the distance in kilometres.
In clear air, lightning can still be seen from more than 100 kilometres away.

teile.einleitung: Volcanoes cannot be stopped, but they can be watched. Experts measure earthquakes, gases and ground movements to recognise an eruption early. This means people can be warned in time.
wichtigste: The oldest volcano observatory in the world was founded on Vesuvius in 1841.
If the ground rises, magma may be rising underground.
Many small earthquakes often point to magma on the move.
An increase in sulphur dioxide can announce an eruption.
Satellites measure ground deformation with radar.
The Volcanic Explosivity Index ranks eruptions from 0 to 8.
Nine centres around the world track ash clouds for air traffic.

abschnitte.text: The **Osservatorio Vesuviano** was founded in **1841** on the slope of Vesuvius near Naples. It is the oldest volcano observatory in the world and still monitors the volcano today. In **1912** the **Hawaiian Volcano Observatory** was set up on the edge of the Kilauea crater on Hawaii. Today it is part of the US Geological Survey. By now many active volcanoes are watched constantly.

When **magma** forces its way upwards, it breaks open rock. This produces many weak quakes, known as **earthquake swarms**. **Seismometers** on the volcano record them. Rising magma also pushes the rock above it upwards. With **GPS devices** and tiltmeters, such uplift is measured to the millimetre.

When fresh magma rises, it gives off more **sulphur dioxide**. That is why experts measure this gas especially often. **Thermal imaging cameras** show hot spots and fresh lava, even through smoke and at night. **Radar satellites** compare images of the same area taken at different times. In this way they detect uplift of a few centimetres over large areas.

The size of an eruption is given with the **Volcanic Explosivity Index**. It ranges from **0 to 8** and is based mainly on the amount of material thrown out. Each level means about **ten times more** material than the one before. Eruptions at the highest levels are very rare.

Ash clouds are dangerous for aeroplanes. That is why there are **nine Volcanic Ash Advisory Centres** around the world. These centres divide the world into areas of responsibility. They track ash clouds and report which airspaces should be avoided. This allows airlines to change their routes in time.

gewusst: Despite all the measurements, the exact time of an eruption usually cannot be predicted.
Some measuring instruments stand so close to the crater that they can be destroyed in an eruption.

teile.einleitung: Clouds are huge collections of tiny water droplets or ice crystals floating in the air. They form when damp air rises and cools down. Clouds bring rain and snow and give away what the weather will be like.
wichtigste: Clouds are made of water droplets or ice crystals.
They form when damp air rises and cools down.
The main types of cloud are called cumulus, stratus and cirrus.
Fleecy clouds look like little balls of cotton wool.
Dark grey clouds often announce heavy rain.
Thunderclouds can grow more than ten kilometres high.
Fog is a cloud that lies on the ground.

abschnitte.text: Air always contains invisible **water vapour**. When warm, damp air rises, it cools down. Cold air can hold less water vapour, so tiny **water droplets** form on specks of dust. Billions of these droplets together make a visible cloud.

Around 1803 the Englishman Luke Howard gave the clouds Latin names. **Cumulus** are heaped clouds that look like cauliflowers. **Stratus** are flat layer clouds that cover the sky in grey. Cirrus are high, fine feathery clouds made of ice crystals. Altogether ten main types are distinguished.

Fleecy clouds look like little balls of cotton wool or like a flock of sheep in the sky. Experts usually call them **altocumulus**. They float at medium height, about two to seven kilometres above the ground. Sometimes they announce a change in the weather.

Clouds look dark grey when they are very thick and contain many large drops, because then hardly any sunlight gets through. Then it often rains heavily soon. The mightiest cloud is the **cumulonimbus**, the thundercloud. It can grow up to the top of the troposphere and brings lightning, thunder, heavy rain and sometimes hail.

Fog is a cloud that lies directly on the ground. In autumn and winter there is often a **sea of fog** over the Swiss Plateau. From mountains such as Pilatus, the Rigi or the Säntis you then look down on a white sea of cloud. Clouds also often form on mountains, because the air has to rise there.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water in the form of a gas, which you cannot see.
Heaped cloud with a white, cauliflower-like look.
Large, tall thundercloud.
Large blanket of fog that looks like a sea when seen from above.

gewusst: A single large heaped cloud can contain several hundred tonnes of water.
Clouds float because their droplets are so tiny that even weak updrafts can carry them.
Aeroplane contrails are artificial clouds made of ice crystals.

teile.einleitung: Weather is the state of the air at a particular place at a particular time. Whether it is sunny, rainy, windy, warm or cold is all part of the weather. It can change completely within a few hours, especially in the mountains.
wichtigste: Weather describes what the air is like at a place right now.
Important weather elements are temperature, air pressure, wind, clouds, humidity and precipitation.
Temperature is measured with a thermometer.
The engine of the weather is the Sun, which warms the Earth unevenly.
Precipitation includes rain, snow, hail and also dew.
Fog is a cloud that lies directly on the ground.
The weather forecast predicts what the weather will be like in the next few days.
Weather is short-term, whereas climate describes the weather over many years.

abschnitte.text: **Weather** happens in the lowest layer of the atmosphere, the **troposphere**. Here it reaches about 10 to 12 kilometres high. Clouds, rain, wind and thunderstorms form there. The Sun warms land, water and air to different degrees, and this sets the air moving.

Temperature is measured with a **thermometer**, air pressure with a barometer and humidity with a hygrometer. The amount of rain is measured in millimetres; one millimetre equals one litre of water per square metre. Wind is measured with an **anemometer**, which spins in the wind. In Switzerland MeteoSwiss runs a dense network of automatic weather stations.

When water droplets in a cloud become too heavy, they fall down as rain. If it is cold enough, snowflakes form from ice crystals. **Hail** forms in thunderclouds: strong updrafts carry grains of ice upwards again and again until they fall down as balls of ice. In Switzerland hail can cause great damage to cars, roofs and fields in summer.

On clear nights the ground cools down a lot. The moisture in the air then settles on the grass as small drops; this is **dew**. If it is below zero, frost forms instead. **Fog** is a cloud on the ground; in autumn it often lies over the Swiss Plateau for days as high fog, while it is sunny in the mountains.

The Alps act like a huge weather divide. It can be raining on the northern side of the Alps while the sun is shining in Ticino, or the other way round. Typical of Switzerland are the warm **föhn** and the cold bise. In the mountains the weather often changes quickly, so you should always check the weather forecast before a hike.

The **weather forecast** says what the weather will be like in the next hours and days. It is calculated with measurements and computer programs. You can find it on television, on the radio, in the newspaper and in weather apps. For the next two to three days it is usually quite reliable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water that falls from the sky or settles, for example rain, snow, hail or dew.
Device used to measure how warm or cold it is.
The average weather at a place over many years, usually 30 years.
Lowest layer of the atmosphere, in which weather forms.
Layer of fog that lies a little above the ground and hides the sun.

gewusst: One millimetre of rain means that one litre of water has fallen on every square metre.
Hailstones can grow bigger than a tennis ball.
When there is fog over the Swiss Plateau, it is often warmer on the mountains than in the valley.

teile.einleitung: Wind is moving air. It forms because the Sun warms the Earth unevenly, which creates differences in air pressure. Wind can be as gentle as a breath of air or as strong as a hurricane.
wichtigste: Wind is air that moves.
Air always flows from high to low air pressure.
Wind strength is often given on the Beaufort scale from 0 to 12.
A storm is a very strong wind that can blow trees over.
The föhn is a warm downslope wind in the Swiss Alpine valleys.
The bise is a cold wind that often blows from the north-east in Switzerland.
Wind turbines use the power of the wind to make electricity.

abschnitte.text: The Sun does not warm the Earth’s surface equally everywhere. Warm air is lighter and rises, and low air pressure forms there. Cold, heavy air sinks and forms high air pressure. The air then flows from **high pressure** to low pressure, and we feel this as wind.

Wind strength is measured with an **anemometer**, and the direction is shown by a weathervane or a windsock. The **Beaufort scale** divides wind into 13 levels from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane force). From force 9 people speak of a storm, from force 12, that is, from about 118 kilometres per hour, of a hurricane. It is named after the British admiral Francis Beaufort.

The **föhn** is a warm, dry downslope wind. The air rains out on one side of the Alps, drops into the valley on the other side and warms up as it does so. Föhn valleys include the Reuss Valley and the Rhine Valley. The **bise** is a cold, dry wind from the north-east that blows through the Swiss Plateau between the Jura and the Alps, especially strongly on Lake Geneva.

A **storm** can uproot trees, tear off roofs and damage power lines. The hurricane-force storm Lothar swept over Switzerland on 26 December 1999 and blew down millions of trees. Depending on the part of the world, tropical cyclones are called hurricanes, typhoons or cyclones. Tornadoes are small but especially violent whirls of air.

A **wind turbine** turns because the wind pushes against its blades. A generator turns the rotation into electricity. In the past people used the wind for windmills and sailing ships. The largest wind farm in Switzerland is on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura, and another stands on the Gotthard Pass.

In autumn children like to fly **kites**, because there is often a good wind then. Sailing, windsurfing and kitesurfing also only work with wind. On Swiss lakes such as Lake Silvaplana in the Engadine there are reliable winds for this. During a storm, however, you should not go into the forest, because branches can fall down.

begriffe.erklaerung: The weight of the air pressing down on the Earth.
Scale from 0 to 12 used to describe wind strength.
Warm, dry downslope wind on the northern or southern side of the Alps.
Cold north-east wind on the Swiss Plateau.
Device that measures wind speed.

gewusst: The föhn can make the temperature in an Alpine valley rise by more than ten degrees within a few hours.
The windsock at airfields shows pilots the direction and rough strength of the wind.
In Switzerland a hairdryer is also called a Föhn, after the warm wind.

teile.einleitung: The Würm glaciation was the last great Ice Age in the Alps. At that time huge glaciers covered large parts of Switzerland. It ended around 10,000 years ago, and after that the present warm period began.
wichtigste: The Würm glaciation is the last cold period of the Alps.
It is named after the Würm, a river in Bavaria.
It began about 115,000 years ago and ended around 10,000 years ago.
The glaciers reached their greatest extent around 24,000 years ago.
The Rhône Glacier reached as far as Wangen an der Aare.
The Rhine Glacier pushed forward as far as the area around Schaffhausen.
In northern Germany the same cold period is called the Weichselian glaciation.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 20th century the researchers **Albrecht Penck** and **Eduard Brückner** described several cold periods in their work “Die Alpen im Eiszeitalter” (The Alps in the Ice Age). They named them after rivers in the Alpine foothills: **Günz, Mindel, Riss and Würm**. The **Würm** is a river in Bavaria. The Würm glaciation is the **last** and youngest of these great glaciations. In northern and central Europe the cold period at the same time is called the **Weichselian glaciation**.

The Würm glaciation began about **115,000 years ago**. It was not equally cold the whole time; the glaciers grew and melted several times. They reached their **greatest extent** in Switzerland around **24,000 years ago**. After that they gradually melted back. Around **10,000 years ago** the cold period ended with the start of the **Holocene**, the warm period in which we live today.

During the Würm glaciation, huge glaciers flowed out of the Alps into the Swiss Plateau. The **Rhône Glacier** covered large parts of the Plateau. Its end moraines lie near **Wangen an der Aare** between Solothurn and Langenthal. The **Rhine Glacier** filled the basin of today’s Lake Constance and reached as far as the area around **Schaffhausen**. The Reuss, Linth and Aare glaciers also pushed far forward.

In the Alpine foothills the **average yearly** temperature was around **10 degrees** lower than today. Today it is about plus 7 degrees there; back then it was below minus 3 degrees. Outside the glaciers there was a bare landscape with grasses and shrubs. Animals such as the **mammoth**, the woolly rhinoceros and the reindeer lived there.

The glaciers of the Würm glaciation shaped Switzerland strongly. They carved out valleys and pushed together **moraines** of debris. When the ice melted, many **lakes** were left behind in the basins, for example Lake Zurich or Lake Constance. Large **erratic boulders**, that is, blocks of rock carried a long way by the ice, also lie on the Swiss Plateau today.

gewusst: Some erratic boulders on the Swiss Plateau come from the Valais and were carried more than 100 kilometres by the Rhône Glacier.
During the Würm glaciation, sea level worldwide was more than 100 metres lower than today.

teile.einleitung: A weather forecast predicts what the weather will be like in the next hours and days. For this, experts collect measurements from all over the world and let supercomputers do the calculations. In Switzerland the federal office MeteoSwiss is responsible for this.
wichtigste: The weather forecast is based on measurements and calculations.
In Switzerland the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, MeteoSwiss, is responsible.
Today forecasts are mainly calculated with computer models.
Air pressure is measured with a barometer.
A high-pressure area usually brings sunny and dry weather.
A low-pressure area often brings clouds, wind and rain.
For more than about a week, forecasts become uncertain, because small measurement errors grow strongly.

abschnitte.text: **MeteoSwiss** is the Federal Office of Meteorology and Climatology, with its headquarters in Zurich. It also has sites in Geneva, Payerne and Locarno-Monti. The office produces weather forecasts, measures the climate and warns the public of severe weather such as storms, heavy rain or heat. The warnings come in five levels, from low to very high danger.

A good forecast needs many measurements. Weather stations on the ground measure temperature, wind, humidity and air pressure with the **barometer**. In Payerne **weather balloons** go up every day, carrying instruments to more than 30 kilometres high. Then there are weather radar, aeroplanes, ships and weather satellites in space.

The measured values are fed into **computer models**. These divide the atmosphere into a grid of many small cubes and use physical equations to calculate how air, heat and water move. This needs very fast supercomputers. The MeteoSwiss models run on a large computer in Lugano. Experts, the meteorologists, check the results and use them to write the weather report.

A **high-pressure area** forms where air sinks. Clouds then dissolve, and it usually becomes sunny and dry. In a **low-pressure area** air rises, cools down and forms clouds and rain. On weather maps highs are marked with H and lows with L (T on German maps).

The atmosphere is a very complicated system. Small errors in the measurements grow bigger and bigger during the calculation. This is called the **butterfly effect**, which the researcher Edward Lorenz made famous. That is why forecasts for one to three days are quite accurate, but for more than about a week they only show rough trends.

Weather forecasts are important for many people: for farmers at harvest time, for pilots, for mountaineers and for people organising festivals. The MeteoSwiss app shows forecasts and warnings for every postcode. A 30 per cent chance of rain means that it rains in about three out of ten similar cases. In the mountains you should check the forecast again just before you set off.

begriffe.erklaerung: A prediction of what will happen in the future.
Device for measuring air pressure.
The science of weather and the atmosphere.
Area with high air pressure that usually brings fine weather.
Device that uses radio waves to detect rain and snow in the clouds.

gewusst: Switzerland runs weather radars on mountains, for example on Monte Lema in Ticino and on the Albis near Zurich.
The barometer was invented in 1643 by Evangelista Torricelli.
Weather services around the world constantly exchange their measurements with each other.

teile.einleitung: A weathercock is a turning figure in the shape of a cockerel that usually sits on top of a church spire. It turns with the wind and so shows where the wind is blowing from. Weathercocks have existed for more than 1000 years.
wichtigste: A weathercock shows where the wind is blowing from.
It usually sits on top of a church spire.
Its beak points in the direction the wind is coming from.
Weathercocks are usually made of metal such as sheet metal or copper.
The cockerel is a reminder of the story of Peter in the Bible.
Below it there are often the letters of the compass points.
In general such figures are called weathervanes.

abschnitte.text: A **weathercock** sits on a rod and can turn freely. Its broad **tail** gives the wind a large surface to push. The wind pushes the tail away until it lies behind the rod. That is why the head with the **beak** points straight into the wind, that is, in the direction the wind is coming from. This shows the **wind direction**.

Below the cockerel there are often four arms with the letters **N, E, S and W** (in German N, O, S and W). This lets you read the wind direction exactly. In general, a turning figure on a roof that shows the wind is called a **weathervane**. They also come as arrows, fish, ships or animals. The weathercock is the best known of them.

abschnitte.titel: High up on the church tower
abschnitte.text: The weathercock usually sits on top of a **church spire**. Up there the wind reaches it easily, and everyone in the village can see it. It is usually made of **metal**, for example sheet metal or **copper**. That way it can stand up to wind, rain and snow for many years. Copper often turns green over time.

The cockerel on the church tower is a reminder of a story from the **Bible**. Jesus told his disciple **Peter** that he would deny him three times before the cock crowed. According to the story, that is what happened. The cockerel therefore stands for watchfulness and for the new morning. As early as around the year **820** a bishop in **Brescia** in Italy had a copper cockerel placed on a church tower.

gewusst: Many Protestant churches in Switzerland have a cockerel on top, Catholic ones often a cross, but there are many exceptions.
The cockerel was also considered a fitting sign because it crows early in the morning and wakes people up.

teile.einleitung: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change is a United Nations organisation that gathers together what is known about climate change. It was founded in 1988 and has its secretariat in Geneva. Governments all over the world use its reports as a basis.
wichtigste: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change was founded in 1988.
It was founded by the environment programme UNEP and the World Meteorological Organization.
Its secretariat is in Geneva.
It does not do research itself but sums up the state of research.
Its assessment reports are written by thousands of experts.
In 2007 it received the Nobel Peace Prize together with Al Gore.
The sixth assessment report was completed in 2023.

abschnitte.text: The **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change** was founded in **1988**, when climate change was becoming a political issue. Its short name is **IPCC**. It was set up by the **United Nations Environment Programme** (UNEP) and the **World Meteorological Organization** (WMO). Its **secretariat** is in **Geneva** at the headquarters of the WMO. Geneva is home to many international organisations.

The IPCC **does not do research itself**. Thousands of experts from many countries voluntarily assess the published research. They sum it up in large **assessment reports**. These deal with the causes of climate change, its effects and ways to slow it down or adapt to it. Each report has a short **Summary for Policymakers**, which the governments approve together.

The IPCC published its **first assessment report** in **1990**. Several more have come out since then. For the **sixth report**, the partial reports came out in 2021 and 2022. In March **2023** the summarising **Synthesis Report** followed. It states that people are clearly causing the warming. Researchers from Switzerland also work on the reports.

In **2007** the IPCC received the **Nobel Peace Prize**. It shared it with the former US Vice President **Al Gore**. They were honoured for their efforts to spread knowledge about man-made climate change. The IPCC reports are also the basis for the international **climate conferences**.

gewusst: The Bern climate researcher Thomas Stocker co-led one of the working groups for the fifth assessment report.
An assessment report runs to thousands of pages and is based on many thousands of studies.

teile.einleitung: A weather front is the boundary between two different air masses. There warm and cold or damp and dry air meet. When a front passes through, the weather often changes noticeably.
wichtigste: A weather front is the boundary between two air masses.
There are warm fronts, cold fronts, occlusions and stationary fronts.
In Central Europe fronts are usually attached to a low.
When the cold front catches up with the warm front, an occlusion forms.
Between the warm front and the cold front lies the warm sector.
The front model was developed around 1919 by the Bergen School in Norway.
When a front passes through, the temperature almost always changes.

abschnitte.text: Air can be very different: warm or cold, damp or dry. A large amount of air with similar properties is called an **air mass**. When two air masses meet, a **front** forms at their boundary. Clouds and precipitation often form there. Behind a front lies a different air mass, so after it has passed it usually becomes **warmer or colder**.

In Central Europe fronts are usually attached to a **low**. They form in the swirl of the low and move across the country with it. First comes the **warm front**, behind which lies the **warm sector** with warm air. Then comes the **cold front**. It is faster and often catches up with the warm front. As it does so, the warm air is lifted off the ground. This is called an **occlusion**.

Sometimes a front hardly moves at all. Neither of the two air masses can push the other away. This is called a **stationary front**. If it lies over an area, it can rain there for a long time. This can lead to **flooding** if the rain goes on for several days.

The model of weather fronts was developed around **1919** by a group of researchers in **Norway**, the **Bergen School**. Its members included Vilhelm Bjerknes and his son Jacob Bjerknes. They were the first to describe lows with warm and cold fronts. They chose the term **“front”** because they compared the clash of air masses with the battle lines of the **First World War**. Their model is still used in weather forecasting today.

gewusst: On weather maps the cold front is drawn in blue with triangles, the warm front in red with semicircles.
A cold front can make the temperature drop by many degrees within a few hours.

teile.einleitung: A pond is a small, shallow body of water in which the water hardly flows. Because it is so shallow, plants often grow all the way down to the bottom. That is why especially many animals and plants live in and around a pond.
wichtigste: A natural pond (Weiher) is a small, shallow body of still water.
A natural pond usually forms by itself, while a man-made pond (Teich) is created by people.
In spring frogs lay their spawn in the water.
Tadpoles hatch from the spawn.
Dragonflies hunt for midges over the pond.
Water lilies and bulrushes are typical pond plants.
The mallard is the most common duck in Switzerland.

abschnitte.text: A **natural pond**, in German a **“Weiher”**, is small and so shallow that light reaches the bottom. That is why plants can grow everywhere in the water. The water hardly flows; it is **still water**. A Weiher usually forms naturally, for example in a hollow with groundwater. A **“Teich”**, on the other hand, is made by people and can often be drained. In everyday life, however, people often mix up the two words.

In spring **frogs** lay their eggs in the water as **spawn**. The clumps of many small eggs float in the pond. **Tadpoles** hatch from them. They have a tail and breathe with **gills** like fish. After a few weeks they grow legs, the tail disappears, and they become little frogs that can go onto land.

abschnitte.titel: Insects on and in the water
abschnitte.text: **Dragonflies** with shimmering wings hunt over the pond. They are fast fliers and catch midges and other insects in the air. Their **larvae** live in the water. The **pond skater** runs on the surface of the water. It is very light and has long legs with fine hairs. That way it does not sink.

The **water lily** is rooted in the mud at the bottom. Its large round leaves and beautiful flowers float on the water. At the edge, the **bulrush** grows in shallow water. It has brown heads that look like sausages and are full of seeds. The plants give animals hiding places and provide the water with oxygen.

The **mallard** swims on many ponds. It is the most common duck in Switzerland. You can recognise the male by its shimmering green head; the female is mottled brown. Because many natural ponds have disappeared, municipalities and nature conservation groups are creating new ones. In this way frogs, newts and dragonflies find a habitat again.

gewusst: A pond skater uses the surface tension of the water, which holds it up like a thin skin.
Dragonflies existed long before the dinosaurs.

teile.einleitung: A volcanic crater is the round hollow at the top of a volcano or on its sides. In an eruption, lava, ash and gases come out through it. When a volcano becomes extinct, a lake can form in the crater.
wichtigste: A volcanic crater usually looks like a large bowl.
Gas and steam often rise from the crater of active volcanoes.
Crater lakes sometimes form in extinct craters.
A huge, collapsed volcanic crater is called a caldera.
The crater lakes in the Eifel are called maars.
Some volcanoes have several craters.
Because of poisonous gases and heat, nobody climbs into active craters.

abschnitte.text: A **crater** is a round hollow that looks like a large bowl. It lies where the volcano’s vent reaches the surface. In an eruption, lava, ash and rock are hurled out here. Even without a big eruption, **gas and steam** often rise from the crater of an active volcano. That is why you often see a cloud above it.

A volcano does not always have only one crater. Besides the **main crater**, many volcanoes have other craters on their sides. Lava can come out there too. In some volcanoes, glowing lava stands deep down in the crater as if in a pot. This is called a **lava lake**. Only a few volcanoes in the world have such lava lakes.

When a volcano is no longer active, **rainwater** can collect in the crater. This creates a **crater lake**. In the **Eifel** in Germany there used to be many volcanic eruptions. In their round craters there are now lakes called **maars**. They formed when rising magma met groundwater and caused violent explosions.

After a huge eruption, the magma chamber under the volcano can empty a great deal. Then the mountain above it collapses in on itself. A huge basin forms, the **caldera**. The word comes from Spanish and means “cauldron”. A caldera can be many kilometres wide and is much larger than an ordinary crater.

Nobody climbs down into the crater of an active volcano. **Poisonous gases** collect there, and it is often very hot. In addition, an eruption can happen suddenly. That is **extremely dangerous**. Only experts with protective equipment sometimes go near the crater rim to take measurements.

gewusst: Some crater lakes are acidic because of the volcanic gases and have a green or turquoise colour.
There are also craters on the Moon, but most of them were made by impacts, not by volcanoes.

teile.einleitung: The water balance shows what happens to the water in an area. What falls as precipitation flows away, evaporates or is stored. With a simple equation you can set these amounts against each other.
wichtigste: The water balance equation is: precipitation equals runoff plus evaporation plus change in storage.
Evapotranspiration is evaporation from surfaces and plants together.
The runoff coefficient gives the share of precipitation that flows away.
On average across the country, a good 1400 millimetres of precipitation falls in Switzerland each year.
Switzerland is called the “water tower of Europe”.
More water evaporates over the oceans than falls there as rain.
The climatic water balance is precipitation minus potential evaporation.

abschnitte.text: For an area the following applies: **precipitation = runoff + evaporation + change in storage**. Water is stored, for example, in **groundwater**, in lakes, in snow or in glaciers. Over many years the **change in storage** often almost evens out and is close to zero. An example: if 1200 millimetres of precipitation fall and 500 millimetres evaporate, then with unchanged storage 700 millimetres are left for **runoff**.

Water evaporates from the ground and from water surfaces; this is called **evaporation**. Plants also release water through small pores in their leaves; this is **transpiration**. Both together are called **evapotranspiration**. The **runoff coefficient** gives the share of precipitation that flows away. On tarmac it is close to 1, on forest soil much lower, because the soil soaks up a lot of water.

The **runoff depth** says how high the water that flowed away in a year would stand if it were spread evenly over the whole catchment area. To work it out, you divide the yearly volume by the area. A river with 10 cubic metres per second carries around 315 million cubic metres in a year of 31,536,000 seconds. With a catchment area of 315.36 square kilometres, that gives exactly 1 metre, that is, **1000 millimetres**.

According to the **Hydrological Atlas of Switzerland**, a good **1400 millimetres** of precipitation falls each year on average across the country. More than half of it flows away, and most of the rest evaporates. The **Rhine**, **Rhône** and **Inn** as well as tributaries of the Po rise in Switzerland. Lakes, glaciers and groundwater store a lot of fresh water. That is why Switzerland is called the **“water tower of Europe”**.

Over the long term, more water evaporates over the **oceans** than falls there as precipitation. The water vapour is carried to the continents and falls there as rain or snow. Via the rivers it returns to the sea. The **climatic water balance** is precipitation minus **potential evaporation**. If it is negative, more water can evaporate than falls as rain. It helps, for example, to assess **drought stress** in farming.

gewusst: One millimetre of precipitation is exactly one litre of water per square metre.
A year has 31,536,000 seconds if you count 365 days.

tgkqsxz.t: WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research

teile.einleitung: The WSL Institute for Snow and Avalanche Research, SLF for short, is based in Davos in the canton of the Grisons. It researches snow, avalanches and permafrost. It also issues Switzerland’s official avalanche warning.
wichtigste: The SLF is based in Davos in the canton of the Grisons.
In 1942 the institute started its work on the Weissfluhjoch.
Since 1945 the SLF has been responsible for avalanche warnings in Switzerland.
Since 1989 it has been part of the research institute WSL.
The WSL has its headquarters in Birmensdorf in the canton of Zurich.
The SLF runs around 180 automatic measuring stations.
It also researches permafrost in the Alps.

abschnitte.text: The institute started its work in **1942** on the **Weissfluhjoch** above Davos. It lies there at 2693 metres, in the middle of the snow. Here researchers could observe snow layers and avalanches directly. Research facilities still stand on the Weissfluhjoch today. The institute is based in **Davos** in the canton of the **Grisons**.

Since **1989** the SLF has been part of the **Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research**, **WSL** for short. The WSL belongs to the federal **ETH Domain**. Its headquarters are in **Birmensdorf** in the canton of Zurich. The SLF in Davos is one of its sites. In this way experts on forests, natural hazards and snow work closely together.

Since **1945** the SLF has produced Switzerland’s official **avalanche warning**. In winter the **avalanche bulletin** appears every day. Using danger levels, it shows how great the avalanche danger is in the different areas. For this the SLF uses readings from around **180 automatic stations** in the mountains. In addition there are observations by experts on the spot.

The SLF researches how snow is built up and why avalanches come down. It also studies **permafrost**, that is, permanently frozen ground in the Alps. If the permafrost thaws, **rockfalls** and debris flows can become more frequent. After serious **avalanche accidents**, SLF experts carry out investigations. From these, people learn how to prevent accidents better in future.

gewusst: The avalanche bulletin uses a European danger scale with five levels.
At the SLF snow is also studied in cold laboratories, where snow crystals can be grown on purpose.

teile.einleitung: In a volcanic eruption, hot molten rock pushes up from deep below to the Earth’s surface. Sometimes the lava flows calmly like a glowing river, sometimes the mountain explodes with enormous force. Volcanic eruptions can destroy whole cities and even change the weather all over the world.
wichtigste: As long as molten rock is below the Earth’s surface, it is called magma.
In an eruption magma rises and comes out as lava, ash and gas.
There are calm eruptions with lava flows and explosive eruptions with ash.
A pyroclastic flow is a glowing avalanche of gas and ash.
In the year 79 AD Vesuvius buried the town of Pompeii.
Many volcanoes lie on the Pacific Ring of Fire around the Pacific.
Etna on Sicily is one of the most active volcanoes in Europe.

abschnitte.text: Deep beneath the volcano, **magma** collects in a magma chamber. The magma is lighter than the solid rock around it and therefore slowly rises. Gases are dissolved in it, similar to the fizz in a bottle of sparkling water. As the magma rises higher, the pressure drops and the gases form bubbles. If the pressure becomes too great, the magma breaks through to the surface.

In an **effusive eruption**, runny lava flows out calmly, as at the volcanoes on Hawaii or Iceland. There flat **shield volcanoes** build up. If the magma is thick and full of gas, an **explosive eruption** happens. Then the rock is torn into ash and hurled kilometres high into the sky. The strength of eruptions is given with the Volcanic Explosivity Index, which ranges from 0 to 8.

The most dangerous are **pyroclastic flows**, glowing avalanches of gas, ash and rock. They race down the slopes at more than 100 kilometres per hour and destroy everything in their path. Falling ash can also make roofs collapse and bury fields. Volcanic gases can be poisonous. When ash and water mix, dangerous mudflows form.

In the year 79 AD **Vesuvius** near Naples erupted. Ash and pyroclastic flows buried the Roman towns of Pompeii and Herculaneum. The Roman writer Pliny the Younger described the eruption in letters; his uncle Pliny the Elder died in it. Under the ash, houses, streets and wall paintings were preserved for almost 1700 years. Today Pompeii is one of the most famous excavation sites in the world.

Large eruptions can affect the whole Earth. In 1991 Pinatubo in the Philippines hurled so much sulphur into the air that it became a little cooler worldwide for one to two years. When Eyjafjallajökull in Iceland erupted in 2010, its **ash cloud** brought air traffic over large parts of Europe to a halt for days, including in Switzerland. Many volcanoes lie on the **Pacific Ring of Fire**, a belt around the Pacific.

Before an eruption, volcanoes often show warning signs: small earthquakes, swelling of the ground or more gas from the crater. Volcanologists monitor dangerous volcanoes such as Etna or Vesuvius with many measuring instruments. This allows the authorities to bring people to safety in time. But even today an eruption cannot be predicted exactly.

begriffe.erklaerung: Molten rock while it is below the Earth’s surface.
Glowing avalanche of gas, ash and rock that races down the slope of a volcano.
Flat volcano made of runny lava, as on Hawaii.
Belt of many volcanoes around the Pacific Ocean.

gewusst: During excavations in Pompeii, people filled the hollows that victims had left in the ash with plaster, making their last postures visible.
The eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 was so loud that it could still be heard more than 4000 kilometres away.
In 1963 an eruption in the sea off Iceland created a brand-new island called Surtsey.

teile.einleitung: A desert is an area where very little precipitation falls. That is why only a few plants grow there. There are hot deserts such as the Sahara and cold deserts such as Antarctica.
wichtigste: A desert is an area with very little precipitation.
The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world.
The Atacama in Chile is one of the driest deserts.
Antarctica also counts as a desert, a cold desert.
In an oasis groundwater comes to the surface.
At night it can become very cold in the desert.
Camels and cacti are adapted to the dryness.

abschnitte.text: A **desert** is an area where very **little precipitation** falls. That is why only a few plants grow there. Not every desert is made of sand: there are also stony and gravel deserts. The largest hot desert on Earth is the **Sahara** in North Africa. It is roughly as big as the USA. The **Atacama** in Chile, on the Pacific coast of South America, is one of the driest places in the world. In parts of it no rain falls for years.

During the day the sun often beats down strongly in hot deserts. Because there are hardly any **clouds**, the heat escapes quickly into the sky at night. That is why it can become very **cold** in the desert at night. Above the hot ground the air bends the light. Then you seem to see water in the distance, but in reality it is the reflected sky. This illusion is called a **mirage** (in German Fata Morgana).

In some places in the desert **groundwater** comes to the surface. An **oasis** forms there. **Date palms** and other plants grow in oases, and people can live there and make gardens. In the past oases were important resting places for caravans crossing the desert with their animals.

Animals and plants in the desert are adapted to the dryness. The **camel** can go for many days without drinking. In its **hump** it stores fat, not water. **Cacti** grow in the deserts of the Americas. They store water in their thick, fleshy stems. Their spines protect them from animals that want to get at the water.

A desert does not have to be hot. What matters is how little **precipitation** falls. Very little snow falls in **Antarctica**. That is why it counts as a **cold desert** and is even the largest desert on Earth. But the snow stays there and over a very long time has become a thick sheet of ice.

gewusst: In the Sahara there are sand dunes more than 100 metres high.
A camel’s humps become smaller and softer when the animal has not eaten for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Volcanic rocks are rocks that form when lava hardens at the Earth’s surface. Because they cool quickly, they are fine-grained or even glassy. They include basalt, rhyolite, obsidian and pumice.
wichtigste: Volcanic rocks form when lava cools quickly at the surface.
That is why they are fine-grained or glassy.
Obsidian is a black, glass-like volcanic rock.
Pumice is full of gas bubbles and can float on water.
Chemically, rhyolite is the same as granite.
Basalt is the most common volcanic rock on Earth.
Columnar basalt forms because lava shrinks as it cools.

abschnitte.text: When magma hardens deep inside the Earth, it has plenty of time, and large crystals grow, as in granite. **Volcanic rocks**, on the other hand, harden at the surface. The lava cools **quickly**, and the crystals hardly have time to grow. That is why volcanic rocks are **fine-grained**. With very rapid cooling, even **glass** without a crystal lattice forms. If some crystals have already grown slowly in the magma chamber, you see large **phenocrysts** in a fine groundmass. This is called a **porphyritic texture**.

**Obsidian** is black, shines like glass and breaks with curved, shell-like surfaces. It forms when lava that is very **rich in SiO₂** hardens so quickly that no crystals grow. In the Stone Age people made sharp blades from it. **Pumice** forms in explosive eruptions: gas-rich lava froths up and hardens at once. The many holes make the rock so light that it **floats** on water.

abschnitte.titel: Basalt, the most common volcanic rock
abschnitte.text: **Basalt** is dark and low in SiO₂. It forms the **ocean floor** and therefore most of the Earth’s surface. Basalt forms at mid-ocean ridges and at hotspots such as **Hawaii** or **Iceland**. As it cools, the lava contracts and cracks at regular intervals. This usually creates five- or six-sided columns: **columnar basalt**.

How runny lava is depends strongly on the amount of **SiO₂**, that is, silicon dioxide. In lava rich in SiO₂, small building blocks called **silicate tetrahedra** link up into chains and networks while still in the melt. In addition, such lava is usually cooler. Both make it **thick and sticky**, and eruptions are often explosive. **Rhyolite** is such a rock rich in SiO₂, pale like granite but fine-grained. Basalt lava, by contrast, flows more easily.

gewusst: The Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland, with thousands of columns, is famous for columnar basalt.
Freshly broken obsidian blades are sharper than steel blades.

teile.einleitung: A waterfall forms when a stream or river plunges over a steep rock step. Waterfalls are loud, powerful and often very beautiful. Switzerland has especially many of them.
wichtigste: At a waterfall, water plunges over a rock step.
When the sun shines you can often see a rainbow in the spray.
Niagara Falls lies on the border between Canada and the USA.
Angel Falls in Venezuela is the highest waterfall in the world.
The Trümmelbach Falls plunge down inside a mountain.
The power of falling water can be used to make electricity.
In winter trained people climb frozen waterfalls.

abschnitte.text: A **waterfall** forms where a stream or river flows over a **steep step**. Often there is hard rock on top and softer rock below. The water wears away the soft rock faster, and so an edge forms. In the Alps, the **glaciers** of the Ice Age also created steep valleys. Today many streams plunge down from their edges.

At the foot of a waterfall the water breaks up into fine **spray**. When the sun shines into the many tiny drops, they split the light into its colours. Then you often see a **rainbow**. To see it, you have to stand with your back to the sun. The spray also makes the air at the waterfall cool and damp.

**Niagara Falls** lies on the border between **Canada** and the **USA**. It is not particularly high, but it carries a great deal of water and is visited by millions of people every year. The highest waterfall in the world is **Angel Falls** in Venezuela in South America. Its water falls almost 1000 metres, so far that at the bottom it often arrives only as mist.

The **Rhine Falls** near Schaffhausen is one of the waterfalls in Europe with the most water. In the Lauterbrunnen Valley in the Bernese Oberland, the **Staubbach Falls** drops almost 300 metres over a rock face. Close by, the **Trümmelbach Falls** roar in a gorge inside the mountain. A lift in the rock takes visitors inside. The **Giessbach Falls** on Lake Brienz are also well known.

Falling water has a lot of power. It drives **turbines** that produce **electricity**. In Switzerland a large part of the electricity comes from **hydropower**. In winter waterfalls can freeze into ice. Then people climb up them with ice axes and crampons. This is called **ice climbing** and is only done with training and safety ropes.

gewusst: The Staubbach Falls is so called because its water turns into fine dust (Staub) as it falls.
At the Rhine Falls you can take a boat to a rock in the middle of the waterfall.

teile.einleitung: The water cycle describes how the water on Earth is always on the move: from the sea into the air, into the clouds, back to the Earth as rain and via rivers back into the sea. It is driven by the Sun. Because the water always moves in a circle, it is not lost on Earth.
wichtigste: When the Sun warms the water in the sea, it evaporates.
When water vapour cools high up, clouds form.
From the clouds the water falls back to the Earth as rain or snow.
The rainwater flows in streams and rivers and in the end into the sea.
Water that seeps into the ground and collects underground is called groundwater.
The water on Earth does not run out, because it moves in a circle.
The Sun is the engine of the water cycle.

abschnitte.text: The Sun warms the water in seas, lakes and rivers. Part of it turns into invisible water vapour; this is called **evaporation**. Plants also release water into the air through their leaves; a large tree can release several hundred litres on a summer’s day. But most of the water vapour comes from the seas. The vapour rises with the warm air.

High up the air is colder. There the water vapour cools and turns back into tiny water droplets or ice crystals on tiny dust particles; this is called **condensation**. Many billions of these droplets form a cloud. The wind often carries the clouds a long way, for example from the Atlantic to Switzerland. On average a water molecule stays in the air for about nine days.

When the droplets in the cloud become too big and heavy, they fall to Earth as **precipitation**. Depending on the temperature, the water comes down as rain, snow, hail or soft hail. In the mountains snow often lies for months or turns into glacier ice over years. In this way snow cover and glaciers store water and release it only later.

Part of the rainwater flows over the surface into streams, rivers and lakes; this is **runoff**. In the end the water flows into the sea, and the cycle starts again. Another part seeps into the ground and collects as **groundwater** in the gaps between gravel, sand and rock. In Switzerland around 80 per cent of drinking water comes from groundwater and springs. Groundwater can stay in the ground for years before it comes back to the surface.

A lot of precipitation falls in Switzerland, because damp air has to rise over the Alps and rains as it does so. The Alps are therefore an important water store for Europe. Water that falls as snow in the Swiss mountains can reach the North Sea with the Rhine or the Mediterranean with the Rhône. On the way it drives hydropower stations. With climate change the glaciers are melting, and the water cycle in the Alps is changing.

You can build a small model of the water cycle. Put a bowl with some water in the sun and cover it with cling film. After a while, drops form under the film and fall back into the water. When a cold mirror steams up after a shower, you are also seeing **condensation**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water turns into invisible water vapour because of heat.
Water vapour cools and turns back into water droplets.
Water that falls from the clouds as rain, snow or hail.
Water that seeps into the ground and collects underground.

gewusst: The water you drink today may once have been part of a cloud over the Atlantic or of a glacier in the Ice Age.
The amount of water on Earth has stayed roughly the same for billions of years.
A large tree can evaporate several hundred litres of water on a hot summer’s day.
